trajectory_summary: This call opens with an unusually technical, engaged customer who runs the rep through a multi-minute roof/panel-count analysis the rep isn't equipped to answer live. The rep survives the technical stretch by eventually deploying the correct scope-discipline exit (bill + design team), then successfully executes the verify sequence and books a next-day phone appointment. The shape is mixed: real credibility cost early, recovered structurally, ending in a clean booked outcome.

observed_outcome.quote: K. Yep. Put you in for 2PM.
observed_outcome.reasoning: Rep and customer agreed on tomorrow afternoon at 2PM for a phone call; a specific day and time were locked. No co-owner was identified (customer confirmed he is the sole owner on the deed with the bank), so co_owner_confirmed is null/not-applicable.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep asked for the utility bill at 07:19 but the customer hasn't moved in yet and has no bill to give; the rep pivoted to square footage (08:00) as a substitute data point, so no actual bill amount or usage figure was ever captured on this call.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never explicitly asked 'what interested you in solar' — the call opened directly into confirming the online form submission, and the customer's motivations (comparing Ion vs. Dominion's own program) emerged organically through his technical questions rather than being solicited by the rep.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: Scope-discipline timing — deploy the escape hatch earlier
primary_coaching_focus.quote: How much panels can you fit in 10 by 23?
primary_coaching_focus.why: Carter eventually made the correct move at 07:19, but let the customer run a multi-minute technical panel-count exercise for three exchanges first, costing credibility (evidenced at 02:48 and the specs-quiz at 05:15) before recovering. The fix is recognizing the FIRST specific technical question as the redirect trigger, not the fourth.

key_moments.quote: immediately gives me pause. You said that, power would be, provided by you guys primarily
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer directly names a trust wobble caused by the rep's own imprecise phrasing, not by an objection they brought in. This is a self-inflicted credibility cost from unclear language about the grid relationship, not a customer resistance pattern.

key_moments.quote: How much panels can you fit in 10 by 23?
key_moments.stewart_read: This is the first clean opportunity to deploy the escape hatch ('that's exactly what our design team maps out on-site'), but the rep stays engaged in the roof-math conversation for three more exchanges instead.

key_moments.quote: I'd love to just get your utility bill so we know how many panels you would need, and then just send it over to my design team.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is the correct move — the rep disengages from a technical debate he cannot win and redirects to the right data point (utility bill/usage) and the right owner (design team), matching the schema's universal escape hatch almost verbatim. It is the single cleanest structural recovery in the call.

key_moments.quote: Yeah. So it'll take me two months to get that to you.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer reveals they haven't moved in and won't have usage data for a month — the rep pivots practically to square footage, but never re-anchors the customer's motivation or creates forward-pulling curiosity about savings once the home is occupied.
